q: How do I calculate process CO2 from limestone or dolomite calcination?
title: Process CO2 from limestone calcination
short: Multiply the tonnes of each carbonate heated by its purity and by its IPCC emission factor: 0.43971 t CO2 per tonne of calcium carbonate, 0.47732 for dolomite, 0.52197 for magnesium carbonate. Then multiply by the share actually calcined. This is Scope 1 process CO2, counted separately from the fuel burnt in the kiln.
audience: Lime kilns, ceramics, glass, steel (flux) and cement plants in India

p: Process CO2 (t) = carbonate consumed (t) x carbonate fraction x emission factor (t CO2 per t carbonate) x fraction calcined.

The factors in Table 2.1 of the IPCC 2006 Guidelines, Volume 3, Chapter 2, are stoichiometric: they come from molecular weights, so they hold anywhere. CaCO3 0.43971, MgCO3 0.52197, CaMg(CO3)2 0.47732, Na2CO3 0.41492, all in t CO2 per t of pure carbonate.

ul: Carbonate consumed: purchase invoices adjusted for opening and closing stock, or weighbridge records of what entered the kiln.
Carbonate fraction: the supplier's chemical analysis or your own lab assay, as CaCO3 and MgCO3 percent. Do not assume 100 percent; Indian limestone grades vary widely.
Fraction calcined: 1.0 unless you can show unburnt carbonate in the product or dust. If you lose kiln dust that is only partly calcined, its CO2 is lower; IPCC gives a correction for this.
Output check: you can also work back from product. Each tonne of CaO formed releases 44.01 / 56.08, about 0.785 t CO2.

sections.h: Which uses count and which do not
ul: Count: lime burning, clinker making, glass batch (limestone, dolomite, soda ash), limestone or dolomite flux in a blast furnace or steel furnace, carbonates in ceramic clay that are fired, and limestone used to scrub sulphur from flue gas.
Do not count: limestone used as a filler or aggregate that is never heated, or CaO bought in as lime, whose CO2 was released at the lime maker.
Do not double count: if a stack monitor already measures total CO2, do not add the calculated process CO2 on top.

p: Report process CO2 as its own Scope 1 line, next to combustion CO2 from coal, petcoke or gas in the same kiln. CBAM monitoring for cement treats them as separate source streams, and a fuel switch cuts only the combustion part.

example.title: Worked example: a lime kiln, one month
lines: Limestone fed: 1,000 t, assay 92% CaCO3 and 3% MgCO3
Total at full calcination: 420.19 t CO2
With 98% calcined: 420.19 x 0.98 = 411.79 t CO2, Scope 1 process emissions
example.note: The coal or petcoke burnt in the kiln is added separately from fuel invoices. The assay and calcination fraction are illustrative; use your own lab results.

senseible: Senseible reads fuel invoices, so the coal, gas or oil burnt in the kiln is calculated from them. It does not calculate the carbonate share: process emissions are calculated only when you supply the measured data, such as tonnes fed and assay.

sources.label: IPCC 2006 Guidelines, Volume 3, Chapter 2 Mineral Industry Emissions, Table 2.1
